{{Short description|Type of polynomial sequence}}
{{inline |date=May 2024}}
{{use mdy dates|date=September 2021}}
{{Use American English|date = March 2019}}
In [[mathematics]], an '''Appell sequence''', named after [[Paul Émile Appell]], is any [[polynomial sequence]] <math>\{p_n(x)\}_{n=0,1,2,\ldots}</math> satisfying the identity

:<math>\frac{d}{dx} p_n(x) = np_{n-1}(x),</math>

and in which <math>p_0(x)</math> is a non-zero constant.

Among the most notable Appell sequences besides the trivial example <math>\{x^n\}</math> are the [[Hermite polynomials]], the [[Bernoulli polynomials]], and the [[Euler polynomials]]. Every Appell sequence is a [[Sheffer sequence]], but most Sheffer sequences are not Appell sequences. Appell sequences have a [[Probability theory|probabilistic]] interpretation as systems of [[Moment (mathematics)|moments]].

==Equivalent characterizations of Appell sequences==

The following conditions on polynomial sequences can easily be seen to be equivalent:

* For <math>n = 1, 2, 3,\ldots</math>,

::<math>\frac{d}{dx} p_n(x) = n p_{n-1}(x)</math>

:and <math>p_0(x)</math> is a non-zero constant;

* For some sequence <math display="inline">\{c_{n}\}_{n=0}^{\infty}</math> of scalars with <math>c_0 \neq 0</math>,

::<math>p_n(x) = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} c_k x^{n-k};</math>

* For the same sequence of scalars,

::<math>p_n(x) = \left(\sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{c_k}{k!} D^k\right) x^n,</math>

:where

::<math>D = \frac{d}{dx};</math>

* For <math>n=0,1,2,\ldots</math>,

::<math>p_n(x+y) = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} p_k(x) y^{n-k}.</math>

==Recursion formula==

Suppose

:<math>p_n(x) = \left(\sum_{k=0}^\infty {c_k \over k!} D^k\right) x^n = Sx^n,</math>

where the last equality is taken to define the linear operator <math>S</math> on the space of polynomials in <math>x</math>.  Let

:<math>T = S^{-1} = \left(\sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{c_k}{k!} D^k\right)^{-1} = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{a_k}{k!} D^k</math>

be the inverse operator, the coefficients <math>a_k</math> being those of the usual reciprocal of a [[formal power series]], so that

:<math>Tp_n(x) = x^n.\,</math>

In the conventions of the [[umbral calculus]], one often treats this formal [[power series]] <math>T</math> as representing the Appell sequence <math>p_n</math>.  One can define

:<math>\log T = \log\left(\sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{a_k}{k!} D^k \right) </math>

by using the usual power [[series expansion]] of the <math>\log(x)</math> and the usual definition of composition of formal power series.  Then we have

:<math>p_{n+1}(x) = (x - (\log T)')p_n(x).\,</math>

(This formal differentiation of a power series in the differential operator <math>D</math> is an instance of [[Pincherle derivative|Pincherle differentiation]].)

In the case of [[Hermite polynomials]], this reduces to the conventional recursion formula for that sequence.

==Subgroup of the Sheffer polynomials==

The set of all Appell sequences is closed under the operation of umbral composition of polynomial sequences, defined as follows.  Suppose <math>\{p_n(x) \colon n=0,1,2,\ldots\}</math> and <math>\{q_n(x) \colon n=0,1,2,\ldots\}</math> are polynomial sequences, given by

:<math>p_n(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n a_{n,k}x^k \text{ and } q_n(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n b_{n,k}x^k.</math>

Then the umbral composition <math>p \circ q </math> is the polynomial sequence whose <math>n</math>th term is

:<math>(p_n\circ q)(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n a_{n,k}q_k(x)=\sum_{0\le \ell \le k \le n} a_{n,k}b_{k,\ell}x^\ell</math>

(the subscript <math>n</math> appears in <math>p_n</math>, since this is the <math>n</math>th term of that sequence, but not in <math>q</math>, since this refers to the sequence as a whole rather than one of its terms).

Under this operation, the set of all Sheffer sequences is a [[non-abelian group]], but the set of all Appell sequences is an [[abelian group|abelian]] [[subgroup]].  That it is abelian can be seen by considering the fact that every Appell sequence is of the form

:<math>p_n(x) = \left(\sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{c_k}{k!} D^k\right) x^n,</math>

and that umbral composition of Appell sequences corresponds to multiplication of these [[formal power series]] in the operator <math>D</math>.

==Different convention==
{{format footnotes |section |date=May 2024}}
Another convention followed by some authors (see ''Chihara'') defines this concept in a different way, conflicting with Appell's original definition, by using the identity

:<math>{d \over dx} p_n(x) = p_{n-1}(x)</math>

instead.

==Hypergeometric Appell polynomials==
The enormous class of Appell polynomials can be obtained in terms of the [[generalized hypergeometric function]].

Let <math>\Delta(k,-n)</math> denote the array of <math>k</math> ratios 
:<math>-\frac{n}{k}, -\frac{n-1}{k}, \ldots, -\frac{n-k+1}{k}, \quad n \in {\mathbb{N}}_0,k \in \mathbb{N}.</math>
Consider  the polynomial 
<math>A_{n,p,q}^{(k)}(a,b;m,x) = x^n {}_{k+p} F_q\left({a_1}, {a_2}, \ldots, {a_p}, \Delta(k,-n);{b_1}, {b_2}, \ldots, {b_q};\frac{m}{x^k} \right), \quad n, m \in \mathbb{N}_0, k \in \mathbb{N}</math>

where <math>{}_{k+p}F_q</math> is the generalized hypergeometric function.

'''Theorem.'''
''The  polynomial family <math>\{A_{n,p,q}^{(k)}(a,b; m,x)\}</math> is the Appell sequence for any natural parameters <math>a, b, p,q,m,k</math>.''

For example, if <math>p=0, q=0,</math> <math>k=m,</math> <math>m=(-1)^k h{k^k}</math> then the polynomials <math>A_{n,p,q}^{(k)}(m,x)</math> become the Gould-Hopper polynomials <math>g_n^m(x,h)</math> and if <math>p=0, q=0, m=-2, k=2</math> they become the Hermite polynomials <math>H_n(x)</math>.
